speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 2 the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) said that the closure of lighthouses off the coast of British Columbia is "proper, sensible and reasonable". He went on to say, "I hate to see the closure of lighthouses, but the world changes and the world moves on".
The Minister did not say, and we have now learned from Transport Canada documents, that the Department of Transport is closing the lighthouses because, according to it, a human life is only worth $500,000 and the lighthouse keepers off the coast of British Columbia only have the potential to save one life every 16 years.
How can the Government say that the number of lives saved off the British Columbia coast does not meet bureaucratic cost-benefit standards? That is absolutely sickening and outrageous. If you could come down from your seat, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you, as a Member for British Columbia, would share that view.
If the Minister of Transport will not save the British Columbia lighthouses for their beauty, heritage, and what they do to protect our coast, I call upon him at least to keep them
open to save the lives that may be lost. Sailors will always be lost at sea, but they should never be lost because the Government cannot find the money to save them and reduces the quotient of human life to a bureaucratic cost-benefit study.

Mr. Speaker, 20 years ago the water rose behind the W. A. C. Bennett Dam to form Willis-ton Lake. Over 150 native British Columbians were flooded out of their homes at or near Fort Graham. Some of these families moved, without compensation or assistance from the federal Government, to Finley Fork and on to Fort Ware. Others moved to Ingenika, some to the Parsnip Reserve, where six homes were built without proper heat or running water, and some to McLeod Lake. In these 20 years the federal Government has done nothing to provide a home, a reserve, or compensation to those flooded out by the Bennett Dam.
The Carrier-Sekani tribal council met with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in Quesnel on Sunday, July 12, 1987, to bring their plight to his attention. They have asked for three small plots of land; 300 acres at Ingenika Point, 200 acres at the mouth of the Finley River, and 1,000 acres up the Messilinka at Black Pine Lake.
In March, 1977, I wrote about this tragedy in B.C. Today. Four Prime Ministers have had this matter before them and have chosen to do nothing. The Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) has represented this area for over a decade and has done nothing.
Now is the time to act. These people are not squatters. They are the original owners and occupants of the land and are treated as beggars in their own land by Parliament. Perhaps the November showing of W-5 will help to awaken the Prime Minister to the reality of the Sekani people.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSSIBLE INCLUSION OF AUSTRALASIAN COUNTRIES
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-POSSIBLE INCLUSION OF AUSTRALASIAN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without a doubt the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States will result in increased prosperity for both nations. Canada will thereby avoid being isolated from the world's trading blocs.
However, let us spare a thought for Australia and New Zealand, countries economically and culturally similar to our own. They could very well face isolation. Once free trade between Canada and the U.S. begins to prove its worth, maybe we could invite the Australasian countries to join also. This would be both to their and our mutual advantage.
1 commend this idea for further study by the four Governments involved.

maintopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TRADE AND TARIFFS
subtopic: DUMPING OF SUBSIDIZED BEEF ON CANADIAN MARKET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the GATT administration has called the countervailing duties, which Canadian cattlemen won the right to impose last year, after the EEC had dumped more than 50 million pounds of subsidized beef on our market, a violation of existing trade rules.
Canadian cattlemen have been hit below the belt again. The EC argued that beef and cattle were not the same thing, and that the application should have been made by the packing plants and not the cattlemen, a pretty weak technical point, but the administration accepted it and ruled against Canada. Unless another international trade committee in Geneva later this month overturns this decision, Canada could see millions of tonnes of European subsidized beef again pouring into our country. There is still hope, as GATT reports must be
approved by both sides and the EC has in the past refused to agree to some panel GATT rulings.
This ruling is most damaging to our cattle industry and Canada cannot afford to let it stand. Canada should say no, no, no, a thousand times no. It is indeed an excellent opportunity to let the world know that we vehemently oppose the heavy subsidization of agriculture carried out by the European Economic Community.

subtopic: NICARAGUA-CRITICISM OF UNITED STATES FUNDING OF CONTRA FORCES
NICARAGUA-CRITICISM OF UNITED STATES FUNDING OF CONTRA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the visit of the Nicaraguan Vice-President is an occasion for all of us to reflect on the obvious sincerity of the collective will for peace which now exists in Central America and which led to the Arias Peace Plan.
The Nicaraguan Government, for its part, has shown good faith through the reopening of La Prensa and Radio Catolica, through unilateral ceasefires in some parts of the country, and through amnesty initiatives. Some of these were either not strictly required by the peace plan or were accomplished earlier than required.
It is now time for the Reagan administration to realize that it must act for peace and drop the idea of continued funding for the Contras. If President Reagan fails to do so and decides that his will is to prevail over the collective will of Central America's political leadership, then all the world will know, as many have long suspected, that it is not freedom the Contras fight for but the stubborn and dangerous reluctance of the United States to permit people it has long dominated finally to determine their own future.

Mr. Speaker, we must respect the New Democratic Party's standing in the polls, and their newly found sartorial splendor. However, let us consider just what kind of Canada awaits us should Canadians grant them the privilege of governing.
To quote from the NDP's 1980 energy policy paper it says: "With respect to (Alberta's) claim that since ownership resides in the provinces they ought to be able to derive maximum benefit from their sale, (the NDP believes) that in energy . .. there is a national interest which overrides a 'what the market

October 22, 1987
will bear' philosophy. There is little doubt that Alberta has already gained substantially from price increases".
If but that were true, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that Alberta lost $60 billion of revenue during those dark days of the Liberal-NDP National Energy Program, a lot of money that could have supported our economy during the lean years of the oil industry and helped to prevent bankruptcies.

PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH BUSINESS COUNCIL ON NATIONAL ISSUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stand as a Member of Parliament who only two nights ago was denied entrance into a private meeting between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the representatives of the BCNI and American people who will be running the Canadian economy.
The Prime Minister had a private briefing with some Chicago businessmen and CEO's from the BCNI. 1 want to say that there is not a single woman who is a representative CEO on the BCNI. Will we allow the Government to ram through a so-called free trade agreement which is nothing more than economic union, and deny Members of Parliament the opportunity to participate in the same kind of briefings that are given to businessmen from the United States? I think it is shameful.
I believe it is understandable that when the Government puts out its free trade document it has the Canadian flag in red, white, and blue because that is where we are heading as a country. The only way we will stop it is if we as a people mobilize on the streets of Canada to let the Government know that this deal will not be rammed through. The business interests will not take precedence over the working people. We will fight it right into the next election.

subtopic: TIGHTENING OF BAIL AND PAROLE SYSTEM URGED
TIGHTENING OF BAIL AND PAROLE SYSTEM URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the brutal murder of Wanda Lee Woodward of Medicine Hat has again focused attention on Canada's bail and corrections system. One suspect was on bail pending trial
on a murder charge. The other was serving time for murder and escaped custody while enjoying a birthday visit to the West Edmonton Mall. This latest incident is but one of many which cause Canadians frustration and anger.
The only punishment available in this particular case will be to deny an already convicted murderer his birthday trip to the mall next year. That is not good enough. In fact it is an insult to the victim, her family and to all Canadians.
I am heartened to note that the Justice Committee is beginning hearings which Canadians have every right to expect will lead to a thorough overhaul of our bail, sentencing and parole provisions. Tightening up on bail and parole for violent offenders will be too late for Wanda Woodward and others. Hopefuly, reform will come in time to save other innocent lives.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF WORKERS' RETRAINING PROGRAM
REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF WORKERS' RETRAINING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Conservative Government is again attacking our senior citizens, especially those who are still working.
After having tried to de-index the Old Age Security pension, after having denied single, separated or divorced people the benefit of spouse allowances, after having cut unemployment insurance benefits paid to older workers, this Conservative Government has announced, through its Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux), that it had eliminated the so-called Workers' Retraining Program, which was actually a pre-retirement scheme. Since August of last year, the Government has cut this program which was available, within designated areas, to 85 per cent of the older workers employed in the textile and footwear industries, and 85 per cent of them were Quebecers.
Since August, the Government has negotiated with the provincial authorities a new but less generous program; the Minister responsible for Income Security has indicated in the National Assembly that he could not agree with what the federal Government had done, claiming that "it should have maintained the former program". Now, because the Government has eliminated this program, 400 working men and women in Canada are on welfare.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly urge all Conservative Members to stand up, defend older workers, and ask the Government to reestablish the WRP, a program which made pre-retirement possible for older workers.

FISHING INDUSTRY-EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian fishermen and the fishing industry have been neglected in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) trade deal with President Reagan. Our fishing communities could be devastated by the omnibus Trade Bill now before the U.S. Congress.
As Hon. Members know, in the groundfish countervail case of March, 1986, the U.S. Department of Commerce ruled that seasonal UIC benefits for fishermen were not a subsidy. However, the proposed U.S. Trade Bill would drastically change these laws and, in future countervail actions, the UI Program could be defined as a subsidy.
There will be a line-up of American fishing lobbyists with countervail petitions. The consequences would be absolutely frightening.
Imagine if you will, Mr. Speaker, the impact of a 15 per cent duty on our fish exports. Why did the Government fail to get protection from this American legislation which could be passed before the free trade agreement even takes effect?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EXPORTS OF U S. SUBSIDIZED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, six times yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that American actions to harm Canadian farmers by stealing our traditional grain markets abroad do not violate the Government's trade agreement. Then he added twice that they may violate the spirit of the agreement, but that that was not the same thing at all.
I want to refer the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the final paragraph of the agreement signed between the two countries, which states:
Accordingly, both Parties understand the need to exercise their discretion in
the period prior to entry into force so as not to jeopardize the approval process
or undermine the spirit and mutual benefits of the Free Trade Agreement.
That is an absolute categorical contradiction of what the Secretary of State for External Affairs told the House yesterday. The official document states in its final paragraph that any breach of the spirit of the agreement pending the final signature is a breach of the agreement itself.
Why did the Minister mislead the House of Commons? Why did he not admit that the Americans have broken this agreement signed between his Government and the Government of the United States?

In a word, no, Mr. Speaker, that is not what I am saying. I am saying that the Export Enhancement Program has been in place for some time. It has been a threat to Canadian farmers. We have been protesting the application of that program. The threat has not in fact reduced the proportion of world markets available to Canadian farmers because of the effectiveness of our marketing agencies and the Canadian Wheat Board as well as the excellence of Canadian agriculture. Nonetheless, this is a measure we want to have removed. We have tried to get it removed before, and the fact that there is now a trade agreement initialled between Canada and the United States will not cause us to stop our efforts to try to get this Export Enhancement Program removed.
As I understand the position of the New Democratic Party, they are saying that because an old subsidy program of the United States continues to threaten our farmers, we should abandon the new trade agreement. Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege to be able to stand in the House of Commons and speak in this debate. In my view, this Meech Lake Accord is so flawed that in good conscience I cannot vote for it. As well, the process of agreement and approval of the Accord has been rushed and is incredibly undemocratic.
I am well aware that my Leader and my caucus have taken a different position, which I respect deeply.
On September 6, 1939, J.S. Woodsworth, the first Leader of the CCF, the forerunner of the NDP, rose in this House in dissent from his Party and had this to say:
The position of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation will be stated at the earliest possible opportunity by one of my colleagues. I say frankly, that with part of that policy I heartily agree, with some portions of it, I cannot agree. Yet I was never so proud to belong to the group with which I am associated.
Grace Maclnnis, former Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, in her book about her father, J.S. Woodsworth, had this to say:
Here was a man who recognized the right to make the decision for the group, yet who insisted on the right of the minority, even a minority of one, to express its own opinion.
So, in my dissent I am following a democratic tradition in my Party.
In my constituency, some 5,000 kilometres from Ottawa, there is a sizeable body of opinion, both within and beyond the New Democratic Party, and in the rest of British Columbia, and indeed Alberta and throughout Canada, which shares my views. I also believe that the Accord of Meech Lake goes well beyond the resolution of the New Democratic Party Convention of 1987 to which I am bound.

October 22, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Let me begin by saying that I too believe it is important to get the signature of the Quebec Government on the Canadian Constitution. However, it is not sufficient a priority that nothing else matters. The real priority is a good and sound Constitution for Canada.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), wanted a deal at any price, and he got one at a great price to the future of Canada. It was not a negotiation. It was in fact a power grab by the provinces. I want to analyse very briefly the result and then go on to some general matters.
First, the Senate of Canada within 14 years will become a provincially controlled body through the power given to the premiers to name the Senators. Either this will be an ineffective process, the new amendment, by the federal Government holding out until it gets its own person on the list, or it will be effective, in which case the premiers will come to love the patronage. It will then be impossible to reform the place or to abolish it.
Eugene Forsey, one of Canada's foremost constitutional experts, and a great Canadian, wrote to me and I want to quote from his letter:
Also, the "temporary" arrangements for the Senate which can be changed only by unanimous consent of the provinces, is, in fact, all the Senate reform we are likely to get. It will give us a much stronger Senate than the present one, as it will have all the present Senate's legal powers, notably an absolute veto over all legislation, and it will have a political clout the present Senate does not possess. It may mean a shift of power from the House of Commons to the Senate. Is this what we want?
The Supreme Court of Canada, which is like a constitutional referee between the Ottawa Government and the provinces, becomes in effect appointed by one of the parties, the provinces. Remember, this is the court that will get new terms to interpret as a result of the Meech Lake Accord such as a "distinct society" as well as old matters such as the extent of the Charter of Rights and the full definition of native rights we put into the 1982 Constitution.
People in British Columbia are waiting to see what sort of names Premier Vander Zalm will put forward. Will they be of the same calibre of the late Chief Justice Bora Laskin or British Columbia's own present judge, Mr. Justice William McIntyre? I believe not. I cannot find a practising lawyer in Canada, not to mention the Canadian Bar Association itself, that likes this provision of the Constitution. This is not the participation in selection of the Supreme Court by the provinces of which the Bar Association spoke, nor what the New Democratic Party policy had in mind. This is the provinces in effect selecting the court.
The Meech Lake Accord constitutionally entrenches a First Ministers' conference, so again power is shifted away from Parliament, the provincial legislatures and the people, to a new super level of government; the 10 provincial barons and the board chairman, the Prime Minister.
Northern Canadians are discriminated against. They will not get a voice in the Supreme Court. They will not appoint Senators. They cannot form new provinces without unanimous permission; of whom? Of the other provinces. There is now a new amending formula requiring unanimous approval of all provinces for reform to federal institutions such as the House, Senate and Supreme Court. Surely this is too rigid.
Many Members in this debate have suggested we could get onto further reform after we hold our noses and pass the Meech Lake Accord. Do they really understand how rigid and permanent it is? All provinces will now indeed have a veto. Women's equality rights, so hard fought for in 1982, have been put in danger. "A distinct society", put in the interpretation as part of the Constitution, is not in the preamble, as we proposed in the NDP congress in Montreal. This could override the Charter of Rights.
Once again we have shut out the aboriginal peoples. Any move to native self-government in the Constitution will now require unanimity of those very provinces that resist the struggles of the native people, or interpretation by a provincially appointed court, the Supreme Court. Let us not lie to Canada's native people and tell them, as Clause 16 of the Meech Lake Accord does, that nothing here affects them. Five years of conferences for the natives, and no luck. Two days for the Premiers and they carve up Canada. Is it any wonder that Canada's original, aboriginal leaders feel a particular sense of betrayal? Jim Sinclair the Metis leader from Saskatchewan correctly predicted last March when he said, "You will look after your own".
Where is the constitutional recognition of the multicultural nature of Canada? Not in the Meech Lake Accord. Provincial power over immigration could result in a checkerboard of immigration policies across Canada and it is being put into the Constitution after little debate and less thought. In the end this could emerge as a sleeper, one of the most radical and controversial changes of them all.
The Accord says that any province can opt out of an amendment, transferring power from the provinces to Parliament and be compensated by Ottawa. I believe this could make such a future power shift in the national interests, for example, broadening the federal authority over financial institutions, less likely.
Of even greater concern is the new power of the provinces to opt out of future federal spending programs in areas of provincial jurisdiction with compensation. Many experts and commentators have said, as well as all the material in the committee, that such legislation as the Canada Health Act, which forced the provinces to stop extra billing by doctors, could not have passed if this Accord had been in effect at the time.
Michael Walker of the Fraser Institute of British Columbia, no friend of the working people, writes gloatingly:
This sort of decentralization is apparently directly anticipated in the Accord and is meant to deal with the coming policy regarding child care.
October 22, 1987

The federal Government would say it wanted to start a national system of child care. Several provinces would say they intended to opt out. The federal Government would then negotiate with them to try to persuade them to stay in. Thus the provinces would get a big share in setting the national objectives of child care, or we could see a hodgepodge of provincial social programs. Either way, Parliament and the federal Government again lose power and the provinces and the courts gain. And who will determine the national objectives? Really, the courts. And who will effectively appoint the Supreme Court? The provinces.
Members should read carefully the brief of the National Association of Poverty Organizations published in April. I used to be a store-front lawyer and acted for this group. There is a group of poor people, and these poor people, especially in my Province of British Columbia, have looked to the federal Government for fairness and help in national social programs. They distrusted the provinces which often take the money and spend it on things other than helping poor people. The poor people know that. They know that instinctively.
Again, the federal Government, in my view, could lose the capacity to deal with effective social programs. This has been given to Canadians as a sort of divine edict, to use Senator Forsey's words, by 11 men who met for two days. Parliamentary hearings were held in Ottawa at the height of the summer, in August, and we are told the whole thing is so fragile, for some unexplained reason, the Government would accept no amendments.
The Prime Minister in his book Where I Stand said that there should be no sessions behind closed doors. He said that Canadians should see and judge those who have been elected to serve them and determine if in the interest of a more generous country they have really answered an urgent and irresistible call to grandeur. If it was true then, why was it not true last summer?
Surely constitutions, which are to last for a long time, should not be made in such haste. Madam Solange Chaput-Roland, in an eloquent plea to the Joint Parliamentary Committee said, "say yes to Quebec". In reality, of course, Quebec is already legally part of the 1982 Constitution and, or course, has been part of the Canadian Confederation since 1867. But I ask you, Madam Speaker, and I do not believe this has been raised in the debate, have the other provinces really said "yes" to Quebec? Or have they just grabbed at power over federal institutions and ran away with those powers?
The provinces received substantial increases in power without a corresponding commitment to uphold the real distinctiveness of Canada, which is a bilingual and bicultural country built on the foundation of the aboriginal people and lately complemented by a multicultural presence. That is Canada. People ask is it not wonderful that Mr. Vander Zalm and Mr. Getty and others have moved a long way from opposing French on corn flake boxes? They are now prepared to recognize Quebec as a distinct society. I say, Madam
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Speaker, that leopards do not change their spots so easily. I believe the opposite is true. Francophones outside of Quebec got nothing, no commitment from the provinces to include their rights. Because of the principle of duality recognized in the Meech Lake Accord, the Vander Zalms can say to the francophones outside of Quebec, "Go home. Go back to Quebec because it is French in Quebec and English in the rest of Canada". That is a tragedy for Canada.
I favour the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society in order to protect the language and culture of Quebec. But the Meech Lake Accord goes beyond Quebec's distinctiveness. This is the essence of the Accord for me. The price paid was to give all the provinces rights in federal powers and institutions: the Senate, the courts, immigration, this broadly-based premiers' conference, the opting out and the spending power. We have weakened the federal Government which, according to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, also has a role in protecting Quebec's distinct society and the French fact in Canada. That role is not just the role of the National Assembly in Quebec; it is also the role of the Parliament of Canada. That was the vision of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
I have heard that we will have harmony now in federal-provincial relations. I would like to point out that conflict in federal-provincial relations is inevitable in our system and can, if it is handled right, be creative. It was not just Trudeau who struggled with the provinces. We can blame it on the personality of the former Prime Minister, as I have heard many people do. But we should be honest. Sir John A. Macdonald, Laurier, King, Pearson and Diefenbaker, all those Prime Ministers, as well as a future Prime Minister, will have to deal with the same thing. It is in the nature of our system.
Meech Lake in fact rejects the basic assumptions of the 1982 Constitution, as well as the 20-year policy of bilingualism and biculturalism. That is why it goes to the fundamentals of Canadian society.
We should think about it in human terms. I have a constituent who I spent some time with last week who is a friend and who has AIDS. He said to me last week, "You know, I am lucky". "You're lucky", I said, "Why are you lucky?" He said, "Because I live here. I have medicare. I have some social acceptance. We have a tolerant society. I have civil liberties. I have a pension from the federal Government which is going to give me a disability pension. I am lucky. I live in the best country in the world if I have to have this horrible disease".
Socialists and social democrats, should look at the whole recent emerging pattern and add to it the decentralization of the Meech Lake Accord to the anti-labour legislation such as Bill 19 in British Columbia, the recent Alberta labour laws, privatization and deregulation, the cruel new immigration laws and, finally, free trade with its north and south continental outlook, especially in energy and in investment. They will see that the Canada that we know, when we look at the totality,

October 22, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
the Canada that we love, the Canada that we fought for, the Canada that we worked so hard to create, is being destroyed. Through the Meech Lake Accord and these other Acts we are creating a different sort of Canada, a less humane Canada. That is why this debate is so important.
I believe working Canadians, if they really had the time to analyse and understand the Meech Lake Accord, would reject it because it is not their vision of Canada. I put it another way.
I	said, look, it is not Team Alberta with Wayne Gretzky or Team Quebec with Mario Lemieux that beat Team Russia, it was Team Canada. This is what working Canadians, ordinary Canadians, feel about this country. Canada is not a country of
II	equal governments or a community of communities as this Accord implies.
Hear, hear!

That vision was rejected in 1982. There is a greater vision, a greater loyalty to a larger entity-Canada. There is a dream of a bilingual Canada where French and English can share this country, or any part of it, anywhere, as equals. This is the dream of Laurier and his tolerant society. It is in the writings of Henri Bourassa. It is the dream of Tommy Douglas who in his speeches said, "But the whole basis of national unity is founded on the principle of equal treatment for all and special privileges for none". That is our dream.
Wake up Canadians. Wake up. Do not be robbed of this vision by some greedy premiers or some wheeling and dealing Prime Minister. Canadians know that. There has been a conspiracy of silence, I have to say, by the other political Parties. Let us be honest with ourselves and fair to working Canadians and their families. In my view they reject a radically decentralized federal Government. They share a greater loyalty to Canada than the sum of the loyalties toward the provinces. That is the flaw in the Meech Lake Accord and that is why it has to be rejected.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest and emotion to what the Hon. Member has just said. I think he made, perhaps unconsciously, a very real point. He said that this is not just Team Alberta, not just Team Quebec, that it is Team Canada.
I listened earlier to what the Hon. Member for Humber- Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) said. I publicly congratulate him here. As a Newfoundlander he came to a decision, he wrestled with a decision, but he wrestled with a decision in favour of Canada. That is what every single Member of Parliament in his or her seat is doing right now and will stand up in his or her place to vote for on Monday at six o'clock. That is Canada. That is what the Prime Minister was saying. The speech the Prime Minister made in the House yesterday will ring down through history, through generations of school children who will know the importance of what he was saying.
I would ask the Hon. Member this. As the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe pointed out, democracy is not tidy; democracy is not perfect. There is no document that has ever come before the House that cannot be amended in some way, that cannot be fine tuned in some way to make it a little more perfect than the imperfect nature of democracy. But I would ask the Hon. Member, and I ask him most sincerely, this. In the interests of a better and stronger Canada, which is obviously supported by the great majority of all Members of Parliament from all sides of the House of Commons, when push comes to shove does he not believe in one Canada, not two solitudes, not three Canadas, not a multitude of Canadas? Does he not believe in one Canada? Will he therefore not have the guts to stand up in his place in this House at six o'clock on Monday evening and vote for Canada?

Madam Speaker, I believe passionately in one Canada. That is why I gave this speech. I believe that people should feel at home, whether they are French or English, anywhere in Canada. I do not think this is one Canada. When I heard the Prime Minister end his speech by talking about one Canada I did not understand it. This is not Diefenbaker's view of Canada, or Trudeau's view of Canada, or Macdonald's or Laurier's view of Canada-
It is the view of all Prime Ministers of Canada.

1 do not think it is. I think it is kind of a wheeling-dealing view of Canada. 1 must say with respect. 1 think it is a view of Canada, which I tried to say in my speech, which is fundamentally flawed because it allows what I call an abnegation of the federal power. It allows the provinces into the very federal institutions where there should be regional representation, perhaps in the Senate, the court, and so on, but it should not hand the provinces this kind of power. I think that will be worse for Canada. It will lead to a Canada that, as I said in my speech, is radically different.
I am not any more courageous than any other Member for speaking out. I do not have the answers either. I am no guru on this particular matter. I respect what the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe said. I respect the Members of my Party who hold their views just as deeply and passionately as I hold mine, as the Hon. Member from Hamilton does, and I know him.
One of the things that bothers me is when the Hon. Member asks me about amendments. I ask him if he will stand up to support amendments when they come forward. I do not think he will. I think he will not because there is a kind of thinking that we have to get this thing through, although it is imperfect, and Member after Member has said that it is flawed and imperfect. I said in my speech that it will be hard to change the darn thing. It will be hard to amend it because of the rigidity in it and because of giving the plums to these provincial premiers who are not going to give them up easily. Those are my concerns.
October 22, 1987

I know the Hon. Member is putting his views as passionately as I am putting mine and that he believes in them as deeply. I guess we fundamentally disagree on this matter.

Madam Speaker, in his lucid and impassioned speech, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) made reference to the possibility that the Accord would lead to a less humane Canada.
He mentioned that he had experience in the anti-poverty movement. It would be very helpful to have from him some elaboration of the thought or notion which he raised in his speech as to what would be the social implication. I suppose he was referring to the spending power of Canada if and when the agreement were to be adopted.

Madam Speaker, there was a notion advanced by some Hon. Members of the House that this would in fact increase federal power because spending power is in the Constitution. My reply to that is no, because it is in the common law and it would have been adopted by the courts if it had been litigated. I do not think we can argue that it is increasing federal power.
However, we can argue that there is a possibility that it may be decreasing federal power and putting future social programs in jeopardy. Jack London, a distinguished Dean of Law at the University of Western Ontario, made that very point. Also, academics have made the point that in fact we may get a hodgepodge of social programs or social programs which cannot be implemented, and that the national objective, as I said in my speech, could be determined by the provinces.
What I was trying to say as a lawyer was that people feel that instinctively. In bad times they look to the federal Government as the equalizer. Western provinces do that too; that is the irony. They look to the federal Government as the kind of over-all thing which will bring equality to Canadians. When they are in need, they know that the federal Government is there. I think they trust the federal Government more than they trust their own particular Governments. Quebecers also look to the federal Government. That is the point I was trying to make.
I gave the example of the new child care program. We will have to see how it develops. However we are putting in jeopardy some social programs, which will hurt poor people and play into a Conservative agenda.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech of the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). We discussed the matter briefly in Vancouver, and I know that he went through a tough time making the decision he has made. I admire him for standing up for what he believes in.
However, I want to understand his thought processes. In 1982 he and his Party supported the Constitution and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. At the time it was brought
Constitution Amendment, 1987
into the House and voted upon, we left out a third of the country. Today we are bringing that third into the Constitution-
We didn't leave it out. Levesque was in power. Have you forgotten?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am speaking to the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway, not to the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), who continually speaks from his seat.
I have a serious question for the Hon. Member. I understand the flaws and I understand his concerns. However, how could the Hon. Member have supported and voted for a constitutional agreement which left out a third of the country and this time, when we are bringing that third in,-and let us put aside the warts-he can rise and vote against it? I just want to know his thought processes.

Madam Speaker, it is an excellent question. The Hon. Member and I always fight and heckle, but we both respect each other.
I remind the Hon. Member that I believe he voted for the 1982 Constitution as did I. Obviously at the time we felt that it was worth doing. Maybe he voted against it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: I voted for it, but I am voting this time too.

In any event his Party voted for it. However, he should be careful with his choice of words. He said that it "left out a third of the country". I was in Quebec this morning where I am living now. Business was going on. People were living. People were paying their taxes, those who cannot afford wealthy tax lawyers. Everything was happening normally in Quebec.
We must remember that it was a separatist Government in Quebec. Did he really expect them to sign? I do not think anyone expected Rene Levesque to sign. We keep forgetting that there were Quebec Members of Parliament in the House and a great majority of them supported it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: And they are supporting it now.

All right, they are supporting it now. However, it was not entirely without Quebec, and I would say that Quebec was legally bound.
It is a good question because it is one of the keys. I suspect-I cannot speak for them; they speak for themselves- that that is the determining factor for many of my colleagues and friends. They are voting for it because they want Quebec in.
The Hon. Member says that I should put aside the warts. I cannot put aside the warts. The warts are too big. To me the whole thing is a flawed vision of Canada. I have been presented with a Hobson's choice on whether or not I want Quebec in.

October 22, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Of course I want Quebec in. I said that in my speech. However, I think we could have Quebec in at a far lower price than this. I think we could have Quebec in without giving the provinces' right to the federal Government. I think we could have Quebec in without fundamentally changing the constitutional nature of Canada as Meech Lake has done, and that is why I am opposed to Meech Lake.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would not want this opportunity to pass without a member of the Hon. Member's own Party having a chance to say that we appreciated and wished to congratulate the Hon. Member on his well put speech-
That is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The Chair does not see how that is a point of order. An Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party had the floor for the better part of half an hour. I allowed other Members to question him and to make comments.
I will now recognize another Hon. Member on debate. [Translation]
Madam Speaker, I am taking part in this debate as it is drawing to a close. I think I may even be the last speaker for the Party I represent in the House. We all know-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: And not the least!

I thank my Whip, and I take this opportunity I have, Madam Speaker-

Since today is the birthday of my esteemed Whip, I hope every Hon. Member will join with me in applauding him.
Hear, hear!

He is young and going strong.
I prefer to start with a smile because I have seen so many people experiencing so much pain as if Meech Lake were to be the end of this great country of ours.
I cannot do otherwise but remember the great courage of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson. He very kindly invited me to accompany him to Winnipeg in 1964 where he spoke to the Royal Canadian Legion. The legionnaires had expected another kind of speech than the one he delivered that day. He told them that the time had come to have in Canada a truly distinctive Canadian flag. He was booed by the entire crowd, with the exception of Mrs. Pearson, myself, Mary Macdonald, his able secretary, and a few legionnaires.
I would say that 98 per cent of them received his speech very badly. According to these people, and if we listened attentively to the speeches in the House of Commons then, the Canadian flag was to be the end of Canada. It was going to destroy the
country. It was going to divide the country forever. I say to you, Madam Speaker, and to these young Pages-because when I give speeches I always talk about the Canada of tomorrow-is there anybody in this country today who would dare say, "Let's revert back and abolish the Canadian flag"? The flag we have today is not the flag that Mr. Pearson proposed. Instead of two red bands there were two blue bands representing Canada's two oceans. The white portion represented the North. Instead of one maple leaf it had three maple leaves, as we see here in our Chamber. As we look up, the maple leaves are there. We can see maple leaves in the Senate Chamber on its ceiling. People seem not to have eyes when they talk about Canada. But there were three maple leaves to represent the three groups of Canada.
Today, Canada is stronger than ever. To believe that the Meech Lake Accord as some colleagues of mine and others have said, will destroy this country is to have no faith in Canadians. Canadians are much stronger.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I agree.

The Chief Government Whip has just said that he agreed. He knows, as I know, that all across this land of ours people will always stand up for one Canada, but a different Canada, a different kind of Canada.
I have seen some of my colleagues agonizing over the Meech Lake Accord because there is a clause that talks about Quebec being a distinct society. This morning, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin), spoke. I congratulated him. He has a better understanding of what Quebec is all about than do many colleagues from other parts of Canada and from other Parties. We are putting into the phrase that Quebec is a distinct society only what is known. I speak now in English, but you know that I come from Quebec. You see from the way I express myself that we really are a distinct society, but I am trying to convey these feelings in English and I will do so in French later on. I see colleagues who are passionately, passionately disturbed as though a distinct society were to lead some Quebecers someday to say, "We will use the term 'distinct society' in order to put up our flag at the United Nations". If that were to be, then I would denounce those words. I would fight again if some people thought that by using the words "distinct society" they could create a new country in the United Nations. There can be only one voice for Canada to speak internationally, and that is Ottawa's. But Canada can have that flexibility and that understanding. The clause is there to take away the fear about disappearing. I know it is difficult for many of my colleagues to understand that feeling. Some Quebecers have no other country. Some came from France 300 years ago and claimed Canada to be their country.
They want to be at ease in Canada, but they fear. They are not chicken. They are not afraid. They fear because there is an ocean of people speaking only English surrounding them. They
October 22, 1987

want some kind of assurance. If they are given that assurance, they will become better federalists and they will become better Canadians. That is what I see in this clause.
This morning a dissident voice in the New Democratic Party said, "I will vote against the Meech Lake Accord." Maybe there will be two or three. Maybe some will be absent.
Mir. Keeper: I hope.

A colleague says he hopes. In any event, the truth will come out. But let me not be distracted. In 1982 the Liberals from Quebec voted yes for the agreement, but very reluctantly. Why did they do so? Why did the majority of us do so in 1982? We did it because it was a step forward again in the Canadianization of our institution. It was to be the end of having to go to Great Britain. We had to amend our Constitution. It was a step in that direction. We were caught between two sentiments. One to say "Yes, I am voting for it". But my province did not vote for the agreement. As a federal Member, a proud Canadian, I voted for it because it was a step like designating my Canadian flag, like designating my national anthem, a step toward being myself, a true Canadian. That is why we said we would vote yes in 1982.
There was another step forward, the Charter of Rights. In our minds the question was whether to vote against that step because Quebec did not or because there were two great new elements. The first was that we had to go to Great Britain to beg its Government to amend our Constitution. The second was the need to have a Charter of Rights. We had to evaluate whether that was more important than the fact that Quebec did not vote yes to the agreement.
The majority of Liberals from Quebec had to make that choice. Yes, it was agonizing I can tell you, Madam Speaker. Yes, we went through long debates. But the agony that most of my colleagues went through then was much greater than the agony that some people are going through today. We had to vote against our own province which did not participate. What helped was a Government there which did not believe in federalism. That made our task easier, I must say. But we paid a price for it. We were accused of being traitors to our own people. It is not the kind of feeling that you like to get every day, but we did vote for it because we believed it was in the best interests of Canada.
As you know, Madam Speaker, my Party has introduced amendments. We do not believe that by voting for that this agreement is perfection or that it is the greatest thing on earth. In no way it is, but it is a step forward, Madam Speaker. We would prefer to have these amendments included.

Who am I, me, Marcel Prud'homme, Canadien-frangais, Marcel Prud'homme-

-a Canadian of French-speaking background. Not Marcel Prud'homme, French Canadian because I am not a French
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Canadian. When will the rest of Canada learn that I am a Canadien-frangais, not French Canadian? I did not translate that into English. In French we all call ourselves Canadiens-frangais. That has been translated by French Canadians so the emphasis seems to be more on the word "French" than "Canadian" in English. While in French we willingly say Canadiens-frangais-so I did not translate. But who am I, Marcel Prud'homme, Canadien-frangais to deny to the native people their own distinctiveness? After all, my ancestors took this land away from the natives. The natives should be recognized. That is why our amendments make sense. I will repeat it in French so people cannot say that we switched something in English that cannot be said in French.

Allow me to ask the question in my own words: Who are we, as French-speaking Canadians living in Quebec, to deny our native people the same recognition that we demand for ourselves? And that is why, even if the Liberal amendment is not included, we wish, together with Quebec, once fully integrated into the Constitutional Act, they will support the efforts made by our First Ministers, including the Prime Minister of Canada, whoever he may be, whether he is the present incumbent or my own leader, when he calls a federal provincial conference on native rights. Then, you will have one major province that will generously support our natives and make it possible for them to obtain their rights just as we are seeking our own. I regret, therefore, that our amendment is not there. I just cannot understand that people do not realize it would be important. It is not included.
Mr. Trudeau himself was a great Prime Minister whom I served loyally from 1968 to 1984, even though I came to the House of Commons before him in 1964. Even he did not get all of what he wanted in 1982. He did not get all of what he wanted in 1970 in Victoria. That would have solved the problem. He played a great part. He did what Mr. Pearson did with the Canadian flag and the Charter of Rights. He did what Mr. Louis St. Laurent did when he abolished the last appeal at the Privy Council in London. That was not antiBritish or anti-English, that was pro-Canadian.
This is always that sentiment which I do not understand. As soon as we are pro-Canadian, we look as if we were antiFrench or anti-British. I am neither because I respect both. Today, I am proud to rise in the House of Commons under a British parliamentary system. I have always defended that system as being one of the best political systems.
My colleague, the Chairman of the IPU, knows of the feeling I express here today, the same feeling I express around the world when I accompany him to meetings of the Interparliamentary Union. I believe in the British parliamentary system. It is part of my Canadian heritage, but I believe also in

October 22, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
la culture frangaise. That is why I feel richer. I have the best from these two great cultures.
People are afraid that the provinces will be consulted on the appointment of judges to the Supreme Court. But, Madam Speaker, I ask you, what is Canada about? Canada did not start with the federal Government. Canada started because of the wish of the provinces to have a superior Government to speak internationally.
I do not despise provincial bureaucrats. I am not scared of provincial Governments. Let's call a spade a spade. I know that some people despise the provincialists. It is as if we were like "father knows best" here in Ottawa and we knew what is good for every part of Canada.
I believe very strongly that Canada is a modern, unique country with provinces which like to be important and with a federal Government that must be important, but there is only one voice that speaks for all of Canada outside Canada. I am not afraid of provincial participation, because that is how Canada was built. It was built because of the wishes of the provinces to have a federal Government and not vice versa.
I am not afraid of the provinces participating. How scandalous would it be if the provinces were to recommend someone for the Supreme Court? Would they recommend dummies because they are the provinces? They will have to be responsible for the people they recommend. They will have to recommend prominent people in their own provinces. I am not afraid of that kind of participation.
I wish we had written this Accord. As my Leader said, if he had been the Prime Minister, he would have negotiated differently. Of course, he is not the Prime Minister. He will go alone Monday night at the time of the vote to give his agreement and I will vote with him.
I would prefer it to be different. I do not like to see the agony some of my colleagues are going through, and 1 believe them to be totally, absolutely sincere. I am not calling them names or saying they are brighter. I am no less a Canadian, and I say this in English, because I will vote for the Accord than those who will vote against it because they think the federal Government is in danger.
I did not come here to reduce the power of the federal Government. If I had wanted to have a provincial career, I would have stuck with provincial politics and tried to make a career there, but I believe in Ottawa. I believe that we can have that ability, that understanding, that comprehension, between the federal and the provincial Governments together.
We have put forward amendments that will respect the multicultural aspect of Canada. Again, this is what is so unique about this country. These provisions will come. I repeat, for the attention of some of my colleagues, who can deny the immense contribution that has been made by new Canadians?
We must understand the evolution of Canada. A land that was not ours was taken by the French settlers, who were then defeated by the British settlers. That is the evolution of Canada. It was a French colony and then a British colony. We had no flag of our own, no national anthem of our own, no Supreme Court of our own. This is the beauty of this country. Without killing each other, without fighting each other, we went through a certain evolution.
I want to commend greatly one of my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), and my two colleagues-

Francophones from outside Quebec have their champions, and I mean first the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier) who is celebrating his birthday today and the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). I can appreciate in all friendship the concern expressed by my colleague from New Brunswick about the survival of the Acadian people. If he feels it is in jeopardy, I share his concern. I can understand what it means.
But I must say-

I would like to repeat in English that I am a passionate believer in a multicultural Canada as it is well defined. Multiculturalism does not mean that there is a division, but one brings to Canada one's heritage to show that Canada is more civilized than any country in the world. We are bilingual not because French and English are nicer than Italian and Portuguese, but because we have French and English for historical reasons. Because we are more civilized than others, we do not want others to lose their cultures. We think it is enriching for the country.
We will be better Canadians and better internationalists if we give respect to people who do not look like us, who do not have the same colour, language or religion. We think this respect is of immense benefit to Canada. Multiculturalism should be part of the Accord, but it will come, as will native rights. It will come, it must come.
Please, let us not believe for a moment that by giving our assent to this we are giving in to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). I am not giving in to anyone. If we want to be partisan, I will say that my Leader spoke first. He opened the door to depoliticization. My friend is smiling, but it is true. My Leader in his great interview in Le Devoir, opened the door to allow the Prime Minister to say: "I can go forward because this man has depoliticized the debate". That is a contribution that we should remember.

Well, Madam Speaker, thank you for-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the Hon. Member have unanimous consent to conclude his remarks?
Agreed.

Thank you, Madam Speaker, for asking my colleagues. I will conclude, for I do not like to overtax the Hon. Members' patience. But I want to tell them that aii those amendments we are hoping for, but which will not pass, will be part of the future. What is not done today will be done tomorrow. Another Prime Minister will have an opportunity to make his contribution to Canadianization and protection. And I would like to repeat that Mr. Trudeau in 1982 was not the happiest man in the world because he did not get all he had set out for, but he gets credit for that gesture of Canadianization. He severed that last British link to allow for constitutional amendments. He gave us a Charter of Rights. That was a tremendous move forward. But Quebec was not there.
Yes, but Quebec was there legally.

There is a colleague there who says Quebec was there legally.

1 do not want Quebec to be in legally only. It does not lead to a constructive participation in the Canadian affair.

In that way, we believe, we can be wrong. I do not question my colleagues' sincerity. There are three here in my own Party who do not share my views. I do not want to have an acrimonious, a passionate debate. I am passionate, that is normal, my country is involved. It is natural that I should be passionate, but I do not want them to believe I am insulting them by having a different view. If it were still possible to convince them that a vote for this will not be such a disaster, if I could still convince them somewhat, maybe our amendments will be put to the vote, we will probably vote for them, and if the amendments do not pass, of course we could wait and abstain from voting. Hon. Members will decide on Monday. But I want to thank you and I want to add that I also would have preferred arriving at something different, but in human matters, one cannot always have everything one would hope for. But I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that when in casting my vote on this issue, I take to heart and keep in mind the feelings voiced by my colleagues on multiculturalism. I say so in French, because I am one of the great supporters, because I understand what multiculturalism means. I do so in Quebec, where this is not as popular as you might think.

I do not do that in English now. I am doing it in French. 1 believe in it.
Constitution Amendment, 1987

I support multiculturalism. I believe in provincial participation. I believe above all that we should have that conference one of these days and make our first citizens, those who were here, Madam Speaker, before you, and I, and even before your ancestors and mine came here to America. Well, I would hope that sometime in the future we complete what we are now doing, as Mr. Trudeau tried to complete what was done by others before him. This is how we built this country. This is how we built Canada, everyone contributing in his time what was possible.
In conclusion, I would like to thank you, and I would like to say I am concluding on the same thought which I expressed at the beginning. If you think it was easy to have a Canadian flag, you should have been here. I was, as a young MP-I listened to all the speeches for months. People said it would be the end of this country. So I ask you to be confident, to have confidence in Canadians and confidence in this country, the same confidence I had when I travelled all over western Canada to convince westerners that a basically Canadian flag would not be the end of Canada. So perhaps by Monday, if we discuss these issues a little more, we may be able to convince some of our colleagues to take a different view. However, I can assure them, especially those in my own Party, that they have my full and unqualified respect, whatever their decision will be. They are just as good Canadians as I am.

I want them to believe that I am as good a Canadian as they are even though we may vote differently next Monday.

If he had a chance to speak directly to the Premier elect of New Brunswick, Mr. McKenna, about his concerns-and what about the Acadians in New Brunswick, in the Acadian peninsula I represent, what should we tell them today?

I thank the Hon. Member. I know Mr. McKenna personally, and I discussed these issues with Mr. McKenna. He has some concerns and so do I. I am concerned about the fact that our native people are unhappy. They are not included in the Meech Lake-Langevin Accord. That is how

things turned out. I don't want to second-guess Mr. McKenna but 1 think he will advise his fellow Premiers of his reservations. We must congratulate New Brunswick because it is the only province which has accepted-

-the rights entrenched in the Charter and the only province to declare itself officially bilingual.

Let us look at what is happening in New Brunswick now. The social climate is much different now than it was 25 years ago when 1 arrived here as a Member. If I could choose what 1 were to be in life I would identify very much with the Acadi-ans. Although I am from Quebec, I have always been extremely active in La Federation des francophones hors Quebec whose champion has always been the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). My colleague is a young Member and could join and become the champion of-

-the rights of Acadians.

I say that in English especially-

-because it must not have been easy for Acadians to survive and to make themselves understood in New Brunswick. Yet, my colleague is now here as an Acadian and he must recognize that the situation has improved because Mr. Robichaud and Mr. Hatfield took some action. Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) and for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) and yourself.
This is why Quebecers should not be narrow-minded. We have to understand that there are a million others like ourselves outside Quebec, and we have to show sympathy and understanding for these people and be able to help them. Quebecers have not done much in the past to help Frenchspeaking Canadians outside Quebec. I can see that the Government Whip seems surprised that I would be so frank, especially in French. In any case-

It is all very beautiful and generous for women of Canada from outside of Quebec to believe that they should protect their little sisters in Quebec. Well, their little sisters in Quebec are way ahead and do not need any protection. They are strong and can defend themselves. 1 dare the provincial Government to touch the rights of the women of Quebec. I can assure you that no provincial Government in the Province of Quebec would dare to tamper with the rights of women in Quebec. Let us call a spade and spade in both languages. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must admit that it is somewhat of an anticlimax for me to rise after such an emotional and passionate debate as that on the Constitution. We are now discussing Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, a very important measure which has thus far given rise to a very serious debate to which I now want to make a modest contribution.
After three years and some months in power, the Conservative Government has finally brought forward for second reading a Bill on the environment.
Before this Bill was introduced, the House and the Canadian public will recall, I hope, that environmental issues had only been debated on so-called opposition days, that is on the days when the Opposition, whether the Official Liberal Opposition or the NDP, propose a debate dealing with the environment.
As we ourselves raised such issues on various occasions, 1 would like to recall briefly the issues on which we proposed debates in this House. We raised the issue of the budgetary restrictions at the Department of the Environment. Hon. Members will recall the many questions that we asked the Government about the cutbacks in certain services, such as the Wild Life Service and the testing done on birds' eggs to determine the level of dioxin and other toxic substances. Then, there were major negotiations on acid rain with the Americans, and we urged the Government to settle the matter as soon as possible to allow us in Canada to maintain our quality of life, our forests, our freshwater lakes, our aquatic fauna which is threatened by toxic emissions from the industrial centres and smokestacks furnaces emitting thousands of tons of toxic substances each day which then fall in the form of rain on Canada and pollute and poison our environment.
We in the Liberal Party have urged the Government to solve the problem of toxic substances dumped in the St. Clair and Niagara rivers as well as in the St. Lawrence, our largest river. I personally asked why we are still allowing the dumping of industrial toxic substances in the beautiful Ottawa River which runs not too far from here and which has been used for a long time as an open sewer by some municipalities. On opposition days, again, we have pressed the Government to support and approve international reports, to support world commissions on the environment and development so that here, in Canada, some positive steps could be taken.
You know, Madam Speaker, the disastrous record of the Conservative Government as regards toxic substances. In November, 1984, as I said earlier, the Government made cuts in the Canadian Wildlife Service, depriving it in particular of its capacity to study the impact of substances on wildlife in order to assess the effects of those products on Canadian health. In November, 1984, the Government cut funds from the Guelph Toxicological Research Centre in Ontario. The
Minister of the day, who fortunately has been removed, had prevented experts from telling the truth to Canadians regarding contamination by toxic substances. The most striking example is the controversy around the contamination of the St. Clair River. The Government stopped publishing Storm Warnings, an important publication which described the movement of toxic substances through air, soil, water, all the way to our food products.
We in the opposition wanted to debate with the Government, here in the House, the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement and the need to hold public consultations on that issue, on the fact that those huge fresh water reservoirs are becoming more and more polluted by reason of carelessness and neglect.
Thus, Madam Speaker, as I said earlier, this is a very important and timely Bill. I am not an expert, an engineer nor a biologist, but a chiropractor. I made a career in that profession. I always have taken a great interest in health, and I still do. I am aware that-
Hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I see my colleague from Kootenay West with whom I studied in 1949 and, as he said earlier, we have been working together for a long time. I remember having studied such important subjects as nutrition and toxicology, which are both matters of national concern. If I am wrong, I stand to be corrected, but the number one concern of Canadians is the quality of life and the environment. Thus, it is not only appropriate but essential that this House pass a Bill with teeth, a Bill that will give us the tools required to clean up our environment and our waters and to get the quality of life that we are all aiming for.
I would like to use this occasion to give an overview of the pollution situation especially as it affects my riding, Ottawa- Vanier. I will talk about the Ottawa River in which toxic wastes still are discharged today. Tons and tons of those substances are dumped in it every year. Sometimes, I watch the Rideau River which flows through my riding and which admittedly is no longer very beautiful to look at today because of all those waterweeds. The phosphates carried by the rain waters which wash or drain the farm lands where large amounts of fertilizers are used contribute to the growth of weeds which deprive the water of its oxygen, asphyxiate the river and cause it to die biologically.
I remember that as recently as two or three years ago, it was discovered by accident on Leeds Avenue, in my riding, that tarry substances had been buried away in the days when natural gas was made from coal. The residue had been buried in the ground. And when the time came to build roads and structures, workers suddenly came across a sticky and terribly polluting mass of coal tar, chemical products and toxic substances that had to be removed at a cost of several million
October 22, 1987

dollars. The same thing happened on King Edward Avenue where a Bank of Canada building was erected on the site of the old Bank of Canada, and when they decided to renovate the building, they found, there again, toxic substances which had to be removed to clean up the environment.
All of this, Madam Speaker, is to indicate that we are quite concerned about the environment and we want powerful means to prevent not only the private sector, but also governments, from polluting. Who does not remember trial where federal Government agencies and departments, the Bank of Canada and five or six other departments and agencies were charged with having dumped-I finally have the list here-last May 12 it was. And I raised in the House the legal proceedings facing the Bank of Canada, the National Research Council, the federal Department of Transport, that of Supply and Services, which had dumped toxic products such as paint strippers, solvents, pigments, hardeners and lacquers into the Ottawa River, in my riding. When they, were brought to justice, they claimed they could not be prosecuted because that area was regulated by provincial legislation. And the judge said: Indeed, the federal level of Government is not subject to provincial environmental laws. If the private sector to which this Bill C-74 will apply .. . and the main purpose of that Bill, if I remember correctly, is to put the burden on polluters and make them pay for damages to us, Canadians, and to society.
Therefore, if the private sector is subject to that legislation, should our governments, including the Canadian Government, not also be subject to the most elementary pollution laws? It is quite normal in my view that the federal Government should be subject as everyone else to measures that prevent and deter polluters and that will chastise, and I repeat chastise the federal Government for those actions that I find absolutely unacceptable, for breaking such a fundamental law as the Environmental Protection Act.
At the time, the Minister answered in this House that the problem would disappear as soon as Bill C-74 was passed by the House. If that is true, Madam Speaker, I am pleased that finally we will have a law with teeth.
But if he had assumed his responsibilities at the time as Minister in charge of Environment, he would have told his colleagues responsible for the Bank of Canada, responsible for the agencies I have mentioned, Supply and Services and others, the National Research Council-our main research body that was polluting with removers, paints and dilutants and other toxic substances-the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) should have told those people: Do not do that, because if you do 1 will slap your fingers. He did not say: Stop that. No, he simply suggested: Wait, Mr. Member for Ottawa-Vanier, be patient. When the Bill is passed we will see to it that those errors are corrected.
Madam Speaker, these are incidents which took place in my constituency that I find sad and worrying.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
I want to speak very briefly about the background of the Act. I know that second reading deals with the principle of a Bill. As I said earlier, the principle of Bill C-74 is to protect the environment and to protect human life and health. This is a rather large Bill that, in my opinion, entails serious responsibilities.
In doing some research about the Bill, I noted that the Act has been amended since 1981. The main concern is that it is not tough enough to allow the identification and assessment of new chemicals before they are used and released in the environment.
The objectives of the amendment, as they were then defined by Environment Canada, were the following: first, identify new chemicals in Canada, because new ones are created almost daily. Second, make it mandatory for users, manufacturers and importers of new chemicals to provide information allowing an assessment of their potentiel environmental and health effects. Third, give the Government the authority to regulate or ban dangerous chemicals.
I want to stress here that that applied not only to the production, here in Canada, of these dangerous chemicals but also to their exportation. Madam Speaker, I know we are not supposed to study the Bill clause by clause on second reading, but if I read the Bill correctly, there is no provision in it that would prevent a Canadian corporation from exporting dangerous chemicals. My colleagues will correct me in committee if I am wrong but I think I read the Bill correctly, and it would allow Canadian companies to produce toxic chemicals in Canada not for use in this country but for export.
The Minister, reacting to those concerns, made all kinds of promises. Everything would be corrected if only we were a bit patient. Madam Speaker, I can find nothing in this Bill that would help clean up the Niagara River, which is important to us, or the St. Clair River. There is nothing in there, that I know of, that would oblige anyone to clean the river up or to reduce air pollution by industry.
In December, 1986, the Minister tabled a Bill or rather a preliminary Bill which had more teeth. The second reading of the Bill was moved on June 11. It was a first step, Madam Speaker. I see that my time is almost up, but I was just starting my remarks.
I will conclude, Madam Speaker, but I am sorry I do not have more time. I would have liked to talk more on a matter of great importance for the quality of our life in Canada. This Bill should be a positive step albeit small, in the right direction. I think that we will support this Bill, but we should realize that it is not the answer to our problems. This Government should not hesitate to move as quickly as possible and show leadership. We would support more important steps in order to clean up our water and give Canadians the clean environment they are entitled to and a proper protection of their life and health against pollutants and toxic substances.

October 22, 1987
Adjournment Debate

Madam Speaker, I listened, as I always do, with interest to the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). He usually presents a clear and factual picture in dealing with any problem about which he is talking or to which he speaks in the House. So this time, Madam Speaker, you can imagine my surprise and my concern when I heard his comments respecting the Government's record in the area of toxic wastes.
The Hon. Member neglected to refer to the fact that within the last year there has been an agreement between the Government of Canada, the Government of the United States, the State of New York, and the Province of Ontario in respect of dealing with chemical dumps along the American side of the Niagara River, which is a major source of toxic waste flowing into the Niagara River and Lake Ontario. Under that agreement there is to be a reduction by one half of the toxic wastes flowing into the Niagara River by the year 1996.
In addition, he did not refer to the funds and efforts made by the Government this year in respect of cleaning up the tar ponds in Nova Scotia. Of course he did not refer to the funds made available and the efforts of the federal Government this year in terms of the clean-up of the Windermere Basin in Hamilton Harbour.
He failed to refer to the fact that right now there is being negotiated-or it has likely been negotiated, subject to the approval of the federal Government and the United States Government-another water quality agreement respecting the clean-up of the Great Lakes themselves.
There has been a very substantial number of steps taken in respect of these matters which the Hon. Member failed to address.
Having been given this opportunity, I am sure he would want to rise now to correct the impression that he has left and to praise and laud the Government for all the steps it has taken to date. I am sure he knows full well that this is only the beginning of efforts by a Government which has only been in office for three years.
When we have been in office for 20 years, as was the case with the former Government supported by the Hon. Member, of course we will have a record which will be some seven times to ten times as good as our record now and thousands of times better than that of the former Government.
