speechtext:
that Bill C-209, an Act to control smoking in public buildings and facilities, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the next 20 minutes I hope to explain, first, why I introduced this Bill, a Bill which aims to control smoking in public buildings and facilities; second, why it is a difficult area in which to get legislative action because of all the competing and vested interests, both private and public; third, to turn in some detail to the nature of my Bill and look at its provisions; and fourth, to look at some of the other initiatives which have also been under way this year on this very important front of dealing with Canada's number one health problem. By the use of that phrase, Canada's number one health problem, I have already indicated the reason that I felt it was important to have legislation such as this before Parliament.
The figures estimated in this country are that 35,000 Canadians die each year from tobacco-related causes. If
35,000	Canadians were dying each year because airplanes were crashing and taking that number of lives, or if 35,000 people were dying from some other disease-and I refer to several which have recently been much featured in the public media for whom the number of fatalities is gratefully so much smaller-you would think that on the floor of this House there would be a tremendous outcry and demand for action. Yet action has been slow in coming.
October 22, 1987

In 1982, the federal health Department warned that nonsmokers are being subjected by smokers to far greater risks than previously believed, including one of the worst cancer-causing substances. The majority of non-smokers seem blissfully unaware of the health hazards due to exposure to tobacco smoke. That was a statement in 1982 of a federal health Department bulletin on chronic diseases in Canada. As a consequence, smokers do not receive enough negative feedback from non-smokers to have a major impact on the problem.
One study of non-smokers in the working environment demonstrated that what is called passive smoking, the inhalation by non-smokers of tobacco polluted air, was equivalent to smoking 10 cigarettes a day. The air of rooms contaminated by tobacco smoke contains carbon monoxide, formaldehyde, many chemicals known to be carcinogens for humans and/or animals and many other noxious and toxic substances. An even greater danger than smoke exhaled by smokers is sidestream smoke that drifts directly from smouldering cigarettes. Smokers' lungs and cigarette filters have trapped some of the worst pollutants, but the so-called sidestream smoke contains those in full strength. The chemical NDMA, one of the most potent carcinogens known, is present in sidestream smoke at concentrations 50 times greater than in mainstream smoke, that is smoke exhaled by someone who is smoking a cigarette. It has produced cancer in all animal species tested by various methods of exposure, including inhalation of a single dose. A non-smoker exposed to air heavily contaminated by tobacco smoke inhales as much NDMA in one hour as a smoker does by smoking 15 non-filter or up to 35 filter-tipped cigarettes. That information was in a 1982 study done by the federal Department of health.
The figures continue to show that each year health-related illnesses in Canada due to tobacco use continue to be serious. As a result, on April 17 I introduced, in the first session of this Parliament, Bill C-287. That was, in fact, the first legislation introduced in the 33rd Parliament to deal with this issue. It was shortly thereafter followed by another Private Members' Bill and a government Bill.
In October, when the second session of Parliament got under way, I reintroduced a Bill, which is in the present form that is before us. Although the other legislation has served in this House and in the legislative committee as a vehicle carrying much of the debate and public discussion of this number one health problem, I wanted to have a further opportunity this afternoon to give Members a chance to debate the merits of this legislation that I have proposed.
This will also give me a chance to put on public record my continuing deep concern about this issue and, indeed, to note that, because of many initiatives taken from different quarters by other Members as well as myself, there is some real progress coming. I say some real progress because-and I come to my second main point-that is an area where it is difficult to get action because of competing interests. There, of course, is the difficulty that Government itself faces with the Department of Agriculture looking out for the well-being of
Smoking Control Act
those in the farming community who are growing tobacco and over the years have received financial assistance from Government to that end, while at the same time the Department of National Health has a large portion of its budget allocated to the health needs of Canadians who are suffering as a consequence of smoke inhalation, direct or indirect. A third vested interest in this on the government side is the Department of National Revenue, which busily raises, through taxes on tobacco products, many millions of dollars that are used to pay both agricultural subsidies and health care costs.
Just as within Government, it is not an easy issue on which to focus because of those conflicts, in the private sector as well. I refer, for example, to an article written last month, in The Globe and Mail's Report on Business magazine which stated that where there is smoke there are profits. The writer goes on at length to talk about the ability of the tobacco industry to stay healthy while its customers get sick. He describes that as being one of the most amazing marketing feats of all time.
There are many millions, indeed billions of dollars, involved in this area. We have arts and sports groups that are worried because they receive in this country some $10 million worth of corporate sponsorship every year. At the same time, there was an advertisement on October 6, again appearing in The Globe and Mail and other papers, organized by the Non-Smokers Rights Association, in which a number of other people speak out on behalf of Bill C-51, people from the arts community. So there is a division there.
Earlier this year in June, a committee of this House of Commons reported that some 500 Ontario tobacco farmers might be forced out of business in the next two years. They recommended that Ottawa divert some of the annual $1.6 billion collected here from cigarette taxes to help producers switch to alternate crops.
I will not take any more of my time going on in that vein. I think you, Mr. Speaker, and others here readily appreciate that it is a very mixed field that we are walking across, with many interests, all strong, all sincere in their points of view, all quite eloquent and articulate in putting their points forward. Yet, in the face of that, there nevertheless remains what I believe to be the important public interest of getting on with some action to deal with the control of smoking in federal buildings and facilities. That is the nature of the Bill I introduced, the one I now want to discuss.
Bill C-209 is not moralistic legislation, it is not puritanical or punitive legislation, it is health legislation. I am looking at this issue in terms of the health consequences on our country. I am trying to deal with the issue in a reasonable way, a way that can evolve toward a better balance between those many interests.
The provisions of the Bill would apply to federal Government premises including buildings, aircraft, trains and the Parliament Buildings. The general rule contained in this

October 22, 1987
Smoking Control Act
legislation is that smoking would not be permitted in any federal workplace or area to which the public has access unless one of the exemptions applied. I contemplate three exemptions: First, when the terms of a collective agreement actually provide for smoking; second, smoking in specified areas designated for smokers; and third, places where non-smoking areas could not be provided because the cost would be prohibitive or major structural changes would be required. In those extraordinary cases, a ministerial certificate granting the exemption would have to be issued on those grounds.
I think this represents a reasonable blend of the interests of all parties concerned: The health needs of everyone, the concerns of non-smokers, the position of those who do smoke, and the financial and physical restraints involved in the Government converting public premises to non-smoking areas. This is what I call the doctrine of reasonable accommodation.
I write my legislation with the doctrine of reasonable accommodation at its core because I think it is important that this kind of legislation succeed. I am mindful of the lesson of the prohibition era, which is that legislation that is drafted too restrictively can in fact be counterproductive. We all know what happened during the prohibition era. The law was just unrealistic and unenforceable in the real world and had consequences that went far beyond what was ever contemplated by the people who initially addressed the health concerns they had about the abuse of alcohol.
Yet health concerns and the public interest do require that we start making some real progress in this area. That is why I wanted today to have this chance to look at some of that progress. There has been a lot of action on this front this year. I will conclude by referring, as I said I would, to some of these other initiatives.
Certainly the introduction by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) on April 30 of Bill C-51 was significant. This legislation would prohibit the advertising and promotion of tobacco and it also deals with the labeling and monitoring of tobacco products. In all frankness, I can say that unlike many people who are active in this area, I do have some reservations about that. As someone who believes fundamentally in the importance of democratic rights and particularly in the freedom of expression, I am concerned that we would prohibit the advertising of a product which itself is not illegal.
I put that on the record because I am not adamant on all fronts on this matter and I think there are serious philosophical concerns about such an approach.
I have no problems with the provision in Bill C-51 for stronger and more visible health warnings so consumers will be more fully informed about the serious hazards of using tobacco products, nor do I have problems with other parts of the legislation. The efforts made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to promote the national program to reduce tobacco use carried out with the co-operation of the provincial health ministries and national voluntary health agencies are very much the way to go in this area.
There has been some real action on a couple of other fronts. Bill C-51 has yet to return to the House, but meanwhile, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) have, for their own part, been taking very positive steps, and I think it is important to put those steps on the public record.
For example, back in May, the Minister of Transport sought comments about the prohibition of smoking on aircraft flights of two hours or less, and that has led to some action. I have here a copy of The Canada Gazette dated September 10, 1987, containing these new regulations which prohibit smoking during flights of less than two hours. These new regulations will be in place before the new year as they can come into effect within 90 days after appearing in The Canada Gazette.
Very simply, the regulations state that no person shall smoke any combustible material on an aircraft operated by a Canadian air carrier on a flight carrying passengers which has a scheduled duration of two hours or less. There are a few qualifications about flights originating outside the country, but that is the main thrust of it. It is also worthy of note that under these regulations, where a crew member is aware that a person is smoking on a flight of two hours or less, the crew member shall-

He welcomes me to run. That is interesting.
I rose to speak on the Member's Bill and I must say I think it is a good Bill and we in the NDP will support it. I liked one of his lines. He quoted someone, and not being Joseph Biden he acknowledged the quote, that the tobacco industry stays healthy while the customers get sick. It is true. It really is a problem but it is being tackled consistently, bit by bit, step by step.
The Hon. Member referred to airlines. MPs do a lot of travelling, especially when you are from the West Coast, and it is a pleasure to be on a smoke-free airplane. I admit it must be tough for those who smoke. I am lucky that I am not a smoker but I feel for them a little bit when they cannot smoke for two hours. I guess through a little law and a little peer pressure they are being forced to give up smoking.
I want to say a few things about the Bill and the general issue. Many Canadians suffer from conditions exacerbated by environmental tobacco smoke. Among those are 5 per cent of Canadians who are asthmatic, who suffer from other lung complaints, who have rhinitis, or who wear contact lenses. Anyone who wears contacts can detect the smoke on the lense and it is a problem. It is of course more serious for those who have asthma or other similar diseases. Smoke is responsible not only for irritation of these complaints but also but because it causes death among non-smokers. I had the Library of Parliament get together some studies on this issue and I want to read from that brief.
Smoking became an issue for non-smokers with the publication of two studies which found that the spouses and children of smokers have an increased risk of serious health problems. One study found that children with parents who smoke experience much higher rates of respiratory illness, including colds, influenza, bronchitis, asthma and pneumonia, as well as reduced lung capacity. A recent federal Health and Welfare study concluded that the risk of lung cancer is as much as 3.4
Smoking Control Act
times greater for non-smokers married to smokers than for non-smokers who are not exposed to cigarette smoke. The same study published in The Canadian Medical Journal found that one in five Canadians has a serious medical condition such as asthma, emphysema, heart disease or angina aggravated by exposure to cigarette smoke. A non-smoker exposed to secondhand smoke in the workplace for 20 years suffers the same ill effects as a person who has smoked 10 cigarettes a day during that period. That is really quite remarkable.
The authors of the report describe airborne tobacco smoke as an occupational health hazard that should be banned or restricted to well-ventilated buildings, but apparently only 10 per cent of the air in most buildings is fresh while the rest is recycled. This means that smoky air is being circulated throughout most office buildings, exposing non-smokers to high levels of toxic and cancer-causing chemicals. Secondhand or sidestream smoke contains higher levels of cancer-causing chemicals than smoke inhaled by a smoker. Unfortunately, air filters do not remove these toxic substances.
I am also informed that in October, 1985, there was a report from Health and Welfare Canada that noted 1,050 nonsmoking Canadians die from lung cancer each year. Lung cancer is one of the most severe diseases, fatal most of the time, and caused by smoking most of the time. Yet over 1,000 people who do not smoke die from lung cancer, perhaps one-half of these because of second-hand smoke or passive smoking. The evidence is there that non-smokers who inhale second-hand smoke also suffer and their rights need to be protected.
The initiative by the Hon. Member is the only way to go. The Government promised a comprehensive legislative approach last year and we did not get one. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) introduced a Bill which would ban tobacco advertising and most tobacco promotion, but never brought it back for second reading. This is just like the former Liberal Minister of National Health and Welfare, John Munro, who introduced a Bill in 1972 which died on the Order Paper. The Government announced a program but it includes no guarantee of smoke-free public or workplaces. The Treasury Board initiated a policy for the federal Public Service but that falls quite short of similar plans introduced by even the private sector. We think the Government should be ahead of the private sector on this issue. The government program does nothing for smoking in public places nor does it cover federally-regulated workers like bank clerks, telecommunications workers, the military or the RCMP.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), introduced a Bill similar in intent to this Bill. It restricted smoking in federally-regulated workplaces to separately ventilated areas. It would provide smoke-free public places, that is the lobby of a public building or bank or a military facility. It said that the workplace of a federally-regulated worker should be smoke-free.

I have only a short time left but this is an important initiative. It is part of a campaign by Members of this House. It is not easy. There is a tobacco lobby which opposes this legislation. That is why there have been delays in the past, probably, in government Bills and so on. However, we are seeing an interesting development in that this comes from a Private Member. It speaks a lot for our reformed House.
As I said, we in the NDP are pleased to support this initiative and I am personally pleased with the initiative put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood.

Madam
Speaker, I looked forward to speaking to this Bill. I have spent 25 years working with young people concerning the effect of smoke and smoking on their lives and lifestyles. I have had some experience with young people and of course adults in that time and I know what it is like so far as smoking or not smoking in public places concerned.
Today I want to confine my remarks to this issue as it affects public transportation and the users of public facilities. There are some advantages and certainly some disadvantages in imposing legal constraints such as those proposed in this Bill. The legislation attempts to accommodate, in their place of work, within reason, both smokers and non-smokers who are employees in the federal Public Service. A problem exists in that some of the people in these public places are not federal employees but employees of the private sector. When the space is shared, it is very difficult to effect legislation which applies only to public sector employees. In such circumstances, legislation such as Bill C-209 could be difficult to enforce.
At present, Transport Canada has in place guidelines for managers and supervisors designed to minimize the harmful effects of tobacco smoke in the workplace. These will remain in place pending consultations with the Public Service unions that will result in smoking being restricted to designated areas by the fall of 1987. Hon. Members will be aware that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) referred to this objective in April, 1987, when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) announced his plans for new initiatives, including legislation, to reduce tobacco consumption by Canadians.
On that occasion it was also announced that there would be continued efforts to reduce smoking by Public Service employees during 1988, leading to a total ban by January, 1989, under a new regulation to be made under Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. It is hoped that these measures will serve as a catalyst and an example to other levels of government and to the private sector.
The Transport Canada guidelines were not intended to invoke a complete smoking ban, nor are they being applied in such a way as to interfere unduly with operational activities by segregating smokers from non-smokers. Instead, they suggest a
number of measures which can be taken to minimize the harmful effects of tobacco smoke which we have heard much about today from the Hon. Member.
Above all, however, managers and employees, smokers and non-smokers, are asked to be guided at all times by practical considerations in the application of smoking restrictions, and by the important principles of consideration and courtesy between smokers and non-smokers. We are starting to see some good signs in this regard. We are starting to see voluntary constraint by the general public, which is becoming concerned about the rights of others. 1 have recently seen more mutual respect exhibited with regard to both primary and secondary tobacco smoke by Canadians in all areas than I have ever seen before in my 25 years of observing this.
The Transport Canada guidelines are intended principally to benefit employees whose work is carried out at a fixed location. Those who operate means of transport, notably the Coast Guard fleet, must deal with their conflicting interests somewhat differently.
The Treasury Board has implemented a policy which prohibits smoking at all service counters, desks, and wickets where the public is served. People are restraining themselves in that regard on their own initiative. They know that their smoke offends some people, and they are withdrawing. It is not unreasonable for the federal employer to require employees who smoke to be subject to certain restraints during normal working hours in buildings and workshops since they are free to smoke as much as they wish once they leave public facilities.
However, the majority of the Coast Guard fleet spend more time at sea than alongside, and it would be unrealistic to anticipate a total ban on smoking aboard Coast Guard vessels. After all, we must realize that the vessel becomes their home as well as their place of work. It is only reasonable that they should be allowed to do on board what they would do on shore.
With regard to transport terminals, restrictions on smoking in public waiting areas and facilities in federally-operated air passenger terminals were introduced in 1982. However, this is a complex issue which, in the case of airports and large railway stations, involves renegotiation of contracts in order to place restrictions in concession lease agreements for shops and restaurants as well as enforcement costs. In these places we are dealing again with agencies and their employees who are not federal employees even though they work in a federally leased space.
Similar considerations apply to railway stations serving other commercial purposes, although there are now some five rail passenger stations that have segregated smoking areas, and VIA hopes to increase the number significantly.
With regard to aircraft, Hon. Members will recall the Minister of Transport's announcement on November 17, 1986, of a proposal to ban smoking on all flights of two hours or less in Canadian commercial aircraft. The proposed new air regulations, which would govern smoking on both domestic
October 22, 1987

and transborder flights, were published in Part I of The Canada Gazette to solicit public comment on January 3, 1987. All comments received have now been reviewed, and publication of Part II is expected later this fall.
These new regulations have been supported wholeheartedly by the Canadian public. I am sure that my colleagues in the House, who travel the airways of Canada as I do, would agree that the smokers of Canada are exhibiting tremendous restraint. They realize that in the confined air space on an aircraft there is limited air circulation. They appreciate the fact that tobacco smoke affects all travellers, whether or not. they are smokers. I believe that the entire traveling public is genuinely interested in complying with these new regulations in good spirit.
The flight to Ottawa from London, Ontario, is of one hour and a half duration and is a no-smoking flight. Virtually everyone on the flight knew that there was a Member of Parliament on board, indeed a Member who is also a member of the Transport Committee, and I did not hear one complaint. I, therefore, assume that Canadians now consider this to be part of their lifestyle and part of their obligation to their fellow citizens.
These new regulations will require Canadian air carriers to post signs prohibiting smoking on such flights and that crew members request any passenger who is smoking to stop. If a passenger does not stop smoking upon request, the air carrier, under the new regulations, will be required to have the passenger removed at the next available stop. I have never seen or heard of this happening. Because of that I repeat that I believe Canadians have accepted this and are working it out on their own. They do not need legislation to force them to do this.
In conclusion, while it is clear that tobacco smoke can be a serious source of annoyance and physical discomfort to nonsmokers, as well as a health hazard to some, it is questionable whether legislation of the kind proposed by Bill C-209 would provide a practical solution to the problem.
I want to talk about self-regulation. We have seen a tremendous growth of this. The Canadian public should be congratulated on their own efforts to control their own lives and develop their own habits. Self-regulation and restriction based on consultations between employees and their managers have so far proved to be an effective means of accommodating both smokers and non-smokers in the workplace. Legislation at this time would probably diminish the context of mutual respect within which new initiatives leading to a total cessation of smoking in federal workplaces are now being adopted.
We should consider that people working this out among themselves are doing an admirable job. I am pleased that federal Departments and Ministers are interested in these matters, but let us not underestimate the Canadian public. Let them decide and work this out on their own.

Madam Speaker, rising in this debate on the Private Member's bill introduced by my colleague, I should like to comment on the possible impact of tobacco smoke on non-smokers and their health. Needless to say, I agree with the previous speaker, perhaps laying more emphasis on the consideration the Government has been giving this issue over the past year and a half, and on the measures which have already been taken. They appear to be satisfactory for the time being and may very well pave the way for further measures which, if I may put it this way, would be more closely geared to individual capability.
It has often been said that tobacco smoke causes untold harm to the health of smokers and non-smokers alike. Canadians are growing increasingly aware of this fact. Scientific evidence concerning the smoke of other people was recently highlighted and explained by American Surgeon General Koop in an article or report on the impact of smoke on the health of non-smokers.
Tobacco smoke contains gaseous particles and products, including in excess of 60 substances likely to cause cancer or other illnesses. According to Surgeon General Koop's report, the smoke from the burning end of a cigarette contains more toxic products and cancer-producing substances than does the smoke inhaled or exhaled by the smoker. In fact, undeniable conclusions of a number of studies indicate that the risk of lung cancer for a non-smoker increases by about 30 per cent if he or she is exposed to the smoke of other people. Smoke from a burning cigarette combined with smoke exhaled by a smoker is a threat to the lives on non-smokers.
When the parents smoke, there are higher risks of pregnancy complications, including infants weighing less at birth and a higher risk of stillbirths. Children of smokers are also more prone to bronchitis and pneumonia than children of nonsmokers. Not only do these children have respiratory infections more often, but they may have a greater risk of developing some type of cancer later.
In a recent report on air transport environment, the United States National Academy of Science describes the dangerous effects of smoke in airplanes and recommends that the United States Congress consider banning smoking in passenger airplanes. In a subsequent report, the Academy also concludes that the risk of lung cancer increases for non-smokers when they are exposed to tobacco smoke. The Academy also notes that children exposed to secondary smoke are more prone to respiratory and pulmonary infections.
Scientific research on tobacco smoke and the health of nonsmokers leads to three general conclusions:
First, involuntary smoking causes disease, including lung cancer in non-smokers.
Second, children of smokers are more prone to respiratory illnesses and symptoms than children of non-smokers. The rate of lung development is lower for children of smokers.

October 22, 1987
Smoking Control Act
Third, separating smokers from non-smokers in the same area can only reduce, but not eliminate the problem of secondary smoke exposure.
Since the Canadian public is informed about the dangers of tobacco and the risk incurred by passive smokers, they are asking for many changes as regards the use of tobacco products in public places. Throughout Canada, in public and workplaces, a special room is reserved to smokers. Municipal and provincial Governments as well as labour and management are taking active steps to change policies relating to smoking in a closed place. The smokers' rights are being questioned when smoke increases the risk of illness for those who share the environment.
At present, our Government subsidizes non-governmental organizations such as the Canadian Lung Association and the Canadian Cancer Society which are actively working for the promotion of a non-smoking society. In fact, those groups of health and public interest play a crucial role to change society's attitude regarding smoking. That is why, as a Government, we intend to continue supporting their efforts.
In October, 1985, the Department of National Health and Welfare, provincial departments of Health and many national non-governmental organizations have announced the implementation of the national program against smoking, another step that will improve the co-operation efforts for a nonsmokers' generation. The program was first aimed at teenagers from 12 to 17 years of age, a vulnerable age when one is most tempted to smoke or to start smoking. The program will also deal with the ever-increasing use of tobacco among the youth, the effects of other people's smoke on non-smokers and the consumption of chewing tobacco or snuff. The program will also try to inform the public about the adverse effects of tobacco and its dependency factor.
Furthermore, new flight regulations proposed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) that would prohibit smoking on domestic and transborder flights of two hours or less, on aircrafts belonging to Canadian airlines, will become effective as of December 9, 1987. Most large Canadian cities have restricted smoking in public places and are gradually adopting increasingly stricter by-laws in this respect. For instance, a municipal by-law passed recently in Vancouver has in fact limited the number of areas where smoking is allowed in most public buildings in that city, including places of work. For instance, if people working in a given department cannot agree on smoking at work, their premises become non-smoking areas by default. Smoking is also prohibited in taxis, retail stores, at service counters and in queues.
This year, Quebec also passed a Bill restricting smoking in various public places. It is the first provincial legislation dealing with this question. The Quebec Bill consists of two parts. In the first part, smoking in government offices, hospitals, schools, public transit and many other public buildings is either prohibited or restricted to certain designated areas. In the second part, municipalities are authorized to
adopt additional measures in this respect in their respective jurisdictions.
The scope of measures to restrict smoking in federal offices has intensified in the past two years. Since no air purifier exists that can filter out both the particles and the invisible toxic gases contained in tobacco smoke, the original plan, which consisted in restricting smoking to specially designated areas, has been changed. The plan is now to gradually prohibit smoking altogether. Consideration had been given to providing independently ventilated premises, but the expense would have been prohibitive. Consequently, the policy announced on April 22, 1987 provides that smoking in the workplace will be prohibited by 1989. During the month transitional period which started on October 1, 1987, smoking will be allowed only in areas specially designated for that purpose. In fact, since August 20, 1987, employees have had to refrain from smoking at all service counters, in waiting rooms, and in offices and at counters where they deal with the public.
No-smoking signs will keep reminding the public of the campaign against smoking.
1 believe it is fair to say that most of us realize the difficulties smokers are facing as a result of these changes. I am confident that we will be able to find ways to achieve the goal set by the Government, which is to provide employees with better protection against involuntary exposure to tobacco smoke in most federal workplaces.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this Bill. Indeed, last night, in a period of an hour's relaxation with my family, I was reminded of the nature of this Bill. I am of that legion of people who are perhaps affected by legislation of this type in that I am, regrettably, a smoker. My wife has the unfortunate habit, in my view, of being able to have one cigarette a month.
I find that frustrating. She may go for several months without having a cigarette. Last night in the presence of our nine-year-old she lit up a cigarette. I think my son demonstrated the unacceptability of that practice by saying: "Mom, you have lit a cigarette. Why?" he challenged her. Why did she do this? She did not need to and he did not like it. That is pretty pertinent. That strikes home, and I am comforted by the fact that children today have this awareness, particularly, in this case, my son Jason.
However, what I must do is to address the context of the Bill before us. Bill C-209 is intended to protect the health of smokers and those non-smokers who are forced to inhale the second-hand or sidestream smoke produced by smokers. Clearly, the best way of protecting smokers is to either kill or cure them.
This Bill was introduced in the House on October 7, 1986. The announcement made by the Government of Canada on April 22 concerning this issue has rendered this Bill redundant.
October 22, 1987

The Minister of National Elealth and Welfare (Mr. Epp), the President of the Treasury Board of Canada (Mr. Mazankow-ski), and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) announced bold new initiatives which go much further than the goals of the Bill we are presently debating.
The Government's initiatives will offer increased protection of the health of all Canadians, not just the health of some of the workers under the federal jurisdiction, as this Bill would do. Let me describe briefly to the House some of the features of the program announced by the Government as they pertain to smoking in the workplace. The issue of workers' exposure to second-hand smoke is, of course, the responsibility of Labour Canada. That is the Department with the mandate to administer the Canada Labour Code, Part IV, which addresses all matters related to the safety and health of workers under the federal jurisdiction. Acting under this mandate, the Minister of Labour has requested all employees under the federal jurisdiction to restrict smoking in their workplaces to specially designated areas. That in itself, I must add, sometimes creates a problem in terms of specially designated areas because you end up with a collection of hardened and committed cigarette smokers all busy burning up their lungs and the oxygen in a very crowded environment, which perhaps in itself will serve as a disincentive to smoking. However, that is only the first step.
The Minister has also asked the review committee, which was established by Labour Canada, to carry out a full-scale technical review of the Canada occupational safety and health regulations, in order to develop a special regulation on smoking in the workplace. This committee is composed of representatives from labour, management and government. It has been asked to have a regulation ready for implementation in 1989.
Lending support to the initiatives taken by the Minister of Labour, the former President of the Treasury Board of Canada, now Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret), announced that the Government intends to ban smoking in all Public Service workplaces by January 1, 1989.
With over 200,000 employees, the federal Public Service is by far the largest employer under the federal jurisdiction. It seems to me that with this kind of support the Government's initiatives will surely reduce the risk from exposure to tobacco smoke in the workplace. I have no doubt that my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), drafted this Bill with the best of intentions. That is the nature of the man and the nature of his work. Unfortunately, it has some deficiencies which are not easy to remedy in a legislative sense.
The most serious deficiency I see is that this Act would not cover all employees who are presently protected by Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. While the word "employer" is defined to include all employers who are presently under the jurisdiction of Part IV of the code, both Section 3(1), which states the purpose, and Section 5(1), which states the application of this Act, would appear to exclude a large segment of employers. All banks would be excluded. Certain airlines, bus
Smoking Control Act
companies, ferries and so on would also be excluded. It seems to me that the logic or fairness of providing health protection to only some employees under the federal jurisdiction and not to others does not lend itself to full endorsement of the proposed Bill.
Another section that concerns me a great deal is Section 6. It is a short section and I shall quote it. It reads:
This Act does not apply in respect of an employee and employer who, by
written agreement, have stated that this Act shall have no application.
The meaning of this section is unclear. Does it mean that an employer can arbitrarily exempt any employee from this Act and permit that employee to smoke at his or her work-station even though that employee may be surrounded by nonsmokers? If that were indeed permissible under this Act, it would defeat the whole purpose of enacting such a piece of legislation.
I do not want to leave the impression that I am against any legislation that would restrict smoking in the workplace. Neither am I saying that there are no worthy features in this Bill. On the contrary, I find the fact that it does not resort to complex and technical measures to solve the problem of smoking in the workplace as being noteworthy. All I am saying is that the Government has not only pledged but has acted upon its promise to take legislative action to restrict smoking in the workplace. I feel that that passage of the Bill before us today will only tend to plant seeds of doubt in the minds of Canadians in terms of whether it is the intention of the Government to proceed further. They will begin to wonder whether the actions taken by the Government are indeed adequate.
I am convinced they are adequate. I am convinced that the initiatives taken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Labour deal with this issue fairly and squarely. So 1 urge my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke- Lakeshore, to bring his ideas on this issue to the attention of the Labour Canada review committee, which I mentioned earlier, and set aside his Bill.
I should like to conclude, if I may, by commenting on the subject of the airlines, which was addressed by two of the speakers in this debate. As do other Hon. Members, I have the need to travel back and forth across this great nation. Being a western Member, my flights are of four or five hours' duration. Quite frankly, I find that smoking or not smoking in a section designated for smoking is really quite unpleasant. If I decide that I do not want a cigarette, that I really do not need a cigarette, I find those around me who are smoking create an unpleasant atmosphere. If smoking were banned entirely on our major carriers, on long-distance flights across this nation, it really would not bother me one iota.

ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-UNITED STATES TRANSBOUNDARY ACID RAIN EMISSIONS/CANADIAN POSITION
['The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, this House stands adjourned until tomorrow at 10 a.m., pursuant to Standing Order 3(1).']

Madam Speaker, it is to acid rain that I would like to draw your attention and that of the House tonight. In particular, I would like to draw to the attention of the House a statement made in the United States two weeks ago when Assistant Secretary of State John Negroponte in speaking on Canada-U.S. acid rain relations told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, first, that emission reductions, which, in other words, means pollution control measures, cannot be defined at the present time; and, second, that the administration's analysis of the document published by a group called NAPAP in the United States shows that the administration in Washington and its understanding of the scientific issues continues to support the policy of the Reagan administration. Mr. Negroponte went on to say that to act now, that is to act by way of imposing pollution control measures in the U.S., could have serious and unnecessary social economic consequences.
Imagine, this is the message from a senior official in the American State Department. Therefore, the question that I have to ask tonight in following up one that I asked of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) a few months ago is whether he will actually admit that despite all the claims made so far by the Government of Canada he still believes that President Reagan will deliver on acid rain and meet Canadian expectations.
His expectations were whipped to an unusual high in this House last April by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on the occasion of President Reagan's visit. His expectations, based on the statement here, have been shattered. What John Negroponte's statement does is this. It reveals that the administration's position on acid rain controls has not changed one bit. It has not changed in the past three years and, by accepting the acid rain envoys' report, the Prime Minister has given President Reagan an excuse for inaction. That was a fatal mistake.
It is worth while putting on record John Negroponte's statement since it reveals a number of things that Canadians in your province, Madam Speaker, in my province and in every province which is downwind to American acid gas pollution should know. In addressing the Senate Foreign Relations
Committee on October 8, Assistant Secretary of State John Negroponte also made these remarks which I would like to bring to the attention of the House.
When President Reagan and the Prime Minister met for their third summit in Ottawa on April 5 and April 6 the President stated, "The Prime Minister and I agreed to consider the Prime Minister's proposal for a bilateral accord on acid rain, building on the tradition of agreement to control pollution of our shared international waters". "It should be emphasized"-and these are the words of John Negroponte- "that in making this commitment, the President agreed to a process, not to a specific outcome".
These are the important key words which must be understood by the Department of External Affairs. They must be understood by the Secretary of State for External Affairs by his Parliamentary Secretary, and by the officials here and in Washington. The Americans have said "Yes, we will consider", and "consider" means just that in English if one looks it up in the dictionary. It means that one considers or looks at a proposition. It does not imply acting on it.
I fault the Prime Minister for having created the impression, in the statements he made after the departure of the President, that the President had agreed to acid rain controls. That was the mistake.
The key words in John Negroponte's comments were that "the President agreed to a process, not to a specific outcome." Therefore, the State Department is leaving its options wide open to do anything that it wants to do.
What does it want to do? We have to look further in the document, issued compliments of the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa, to find the following:
The administration's position is also clear. There is a significant long term concern, but, in view of our present understanding and remaining scientific and technical uncertainties, the need for or form of, additional emissions reductions cannot be defined at the present time.
Imagine that!
John Negroponte went on to say:
The administration is prepared to take further action, as necessary, as the uncertainties are resolved. The recently released interim report presents the current state of knowledge about half way through the NAPAP's ten year scientific investigations of the problem. The administration's analysis of this document shows that our understanding-
"Our" meaning that of the State Department. He continued:
-of the scientific issues continues to support our policies. To act now, in the face of these uncertainties, could have serious and unnecessary socioeconomic consequences.
Imagine, that is the thinking of the State Department. They are light-years behind what goes on out there in the environment. They do not understand the consequences to our ecosystem or our resources.
October 22, 1987

I will be very happy to hear the interpretation the Parliamentary Secretary would like to give us on this very significant and unfortunate statement.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, obviously and in the mind of this Government there is no doubt that acid rain remains the most serious environmental issue between Canada and the U.S.A. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made acid rain one of the principal subjects of discussion when President Reagan visited Ottawa in April. At the Prime Minister's urging, the President agreed-and all Canadians will agree-to consider the Prime Minister's proposal for a bilateral accord on acid rain.
The resolve and persistence of the Government have been amply and repeatedly demonstrated. The Hon. Tom McMillan, the Minister of the Environment, has spoken out on acid rain forcefully in the United States and Canada. The release by the United States of the unsatisfactory executive summary of the National Acidic Precipitation Assessment Program Report was met with a vigorous and firm response. In June, the Parliamentary Committee on Acid Rain, under the able chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Parry Sound- Muskoka (Mr. Darling), visited Washington and presented the Canadian case. From the beginning, our aims have been clear. We seek to remove a threat to the Canadian environment. We aim to achieve something, not just demand it.
Our objectives on acid rain have been clearly and repeatedly stated, but let me repeat them again for the Hon. Member. Canada wants a bilateral Accord that specifies targets and schedules necessary to prevent the damage caused by the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide. Broadly speaking, we believe that a level of sulphur deposition which our environment can safely sustain will be reached when two things happen: Our national acid rain abatement program reduces annual Canadian-origin deposition levels in eastern Canada to no more than 2.3 million tonnes-an objective we should achieve by 1994; and the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide from the United States is reduced to no more than 2 million tonnes annually.
Madam Speaker, there is nothing mysterious or hidden in any of this. We have an environment that needs to be protected; a scientifically sound target level at which the necessary protection will be achieved; a domestic abatement program to deal with that half of the problem which is of our own making; and a negotiating strategy to address the part of the problem that originates in the United States.
In discussions with American officials since the President's announcement in April, Canadian officials have enunciated our approach clearly. I can assure the House that the Government and its officials are resolved to pursue this opportunity as effectively as we can and to achieve something that answers the needs of the Canadian environment.
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: ROAD SAFETY-NATIONAL SAFETY CODE FOR TRUCKING
ROAD SAFETY-NATIONAL SAFETY CODE FOR TRUCKING
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to rise on this occasion and speak on behalf of the constituents of London-Middlesex-an area which is one of the transportation hubs of Canada-to talk about our concerns. It was very interesting, in fact enlightening when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) answered my query about a national safety code when I was worried about killer trucks on the highways of the United States and the potential of them doing damage on Canadian roads. I wondered what his reaction would be and that of his colleagues, the Ministers of Transport in the provinces and the territories.
I was delighted when he answered that there would be a national safety code. The Ministers agreed to a national safety code which will be effective for Canada January 1, 1988. In fact, Madam Speaker, the Minister went further and said that the Ministers agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding committing themselves to the implementation of it and agreed to a timetable which would be phased in by 1990. Further, they gave their approval to a cost sharing formula for the development and implementation of the code, including the establishment of a national computer link which would permit all jurisdictions to take timely action against unsafe conduct of the operators of commercial vehicles regardless of where an offence is committed in Canada.
It looked like safety was well on its way to being looked after in Canada. However, I have one or two concerns from my question to the Minister and I would like to address them. It would appear to me and certainly to my constituents that the national safety code is dependent upon uniform implementation across the country. The truckers and those involved in this field of transportation in my riding feel that some degree of provincial flexibility might be desirable but, nonetheless, common sense must prevail.
If there are certain provinces which do not meet the time frame proposed in the Memorandum of Understanding, it will lead to the possibility that the federal law would prove invalid since it would not be applied equally across the country. It seems, therefore, that provincial co-operation is crucial in getting this program off the ground. My constituents feel that unless there is more co-ordination a great opportunity will be lost. The regulations would merely exist on paper and could not be enforced. In fact, my constituents have some very specific questions which they would like me to address to the Minister because they are inherent in what has to happen.
What is the current status of negotiation with the provinces? Will there be a significant level of uniformity across Canada? This is very important, Madam Speaker. How can we have

October 22, 1987
Adjournment Debate
trade of goods from coast to coast if we do not have a transportation system and policies which will allow us to be competitive? We realize that there are different roadbeds with different carrying capabilities from province to province and we know there will be difficulties. We are not sure what that will lead to in terms of uniformity.
Some degree of uniformity is required from coast to coast. If there is no uniformity, it will be difficult to enforce the federal law. In fact, it may even prove to be unconstitutional. Are the provinces essentially pursuing their own regulations and resisting attempts to establish some common ground which a national code needs and in fact on which a national code is founded?
We realize that some provinces have very distinct problems with road designs and road widths and inclines which all affect the weight and the length of transports which can be applied to the roads in those provinces. We realize that there are great differences in the roads, but given that, what will happen to the ability of the provinces to have the required regulations put in place? How does this affect the national safety code's scheduled implementation date? Will this delay or in fact put to rest a uniform transportation system for goods and services from coast to coast?
This is indeed very important. It is just one aspect of the new legislation which the Government put in place under Bill C-19 which became law this fall. Canadians want safety on their roads, but they also want a very efficient transportation system.
The truckers, the people who provide this system for Canadians, want to be competitive with our friends south of the border. They do not want to have to give up their businesses to the Americans. They want to be competitive so they want to know what the National Safety Code is all about and if it will be applied uniformly in all provinces and therefore what they have to do to measure up.
I hope that the Minister can enlighten us on the national safety code, which was a great vision. Where is it today and what can Canadian truckers expect tomorrow?

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Clinch (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: ROAD SAFETY-NATIONAL SAFETY CODE FOR TRUCKING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to the Hon. Member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Clifford). The national safety code for motor carriers basically consists of two components. The first defines minimum safety standards and practices for drivers, carriers and vehicles. The second defines government standards which are necessary for enforcement purposes to ensure industry compliance with the national safety code.
The code will be phased in over a two-year period commencing on January 1, 1988, with full implementation expected by January 1, 1990. The phase-in approach is due to the provincial legislative requirements which are necessary for implementation of certain national safety code standards.
I would like to assure the Hon. Member that most parts of the code will be in place in most provinces by January of 1988. I would also like the Hon. Member to know that the federal Government contributed $24 million to the developmental costs of the code.
It should be noted that a number of standards are already in place today such as the single driver's licence concept, the classified driver's licence system and security of load, just to name a few. The federal Government and all provincial jurisdictions agree that a national safety code is paramount to ensuring that safety on our highways does not decrease as a result of regulatory reform. All concerned have committed themselves to continue their diligent work on the development of a uniform National Safety Code for Canada and to ensure that the timetable for implementation of the code is met.
